articles.title: Tracking multidrug resistant tuberculosis: a 30-year analysis of global, regional, and national trends.
articles.snippet: Song HW, Tian JH, Song HP, Guo SJ, Lin YH, Pan JS | Frontiers in public health | 2024 | Journal Article
articles.full_summary: MDR-TB remains a global health concern, particularly in lower socio-demographic index regions, with incidence rates showing a steadfast presence over the past decade and a troubling forecast predicting an uptick from 2020 to 2030.
articles.key_finding: Notably, the incidence rates have shown a steadfast presence over the past decade, and a troubling forecast predicts an uptick in these areas from 2020 to 2030.

articles.title: Global, regional, and national burden of HIV-negative tuberculosis, 1990-2021: findings from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021.
articles.snippet: Zhang SX, Miao FY, Yang J, Zhou WT, Lv S, Wei FN et al. | Infectious diseases of poverty | 2024-Aug-19 | Journal Article
articles.full_summary: This study examines the epidemiological characteristics of HIV-negative TB globally, including MDR-TB and XDR-TB, from 1990 to 2021, and projects trends to 2035, highlighting an upward trend in drug-resistant TB.
articles.key_finding: The global ASIR of MDR-TB has not decreased since 2015, instead, it has shown a slow upward trend in recent years. The ASIR of XDR-TB has exhibited significant increase in the past 30 years. The projections indicate MDR-TB and XDR-TB are expected to see significant increases in both ASIR and ASMR from 2022 to 2035, highlighting the growing challenge of drug-resistant TB.

articles.title: Global and regional trends in multidrug- or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis, 2000-2024 with forecasts to 2030: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.snippet: Hossain A, Asmar AE, Almheiri A, Almheiri H, Alameddine M | BMC infectious diseases | 2026-Apr-20 | Systematic Review; Journal Article; Meta-Analysis
articles.full_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis assesses global and regional trends in MDR/RR-TB prevalence from 2000 to 2024, with forecasts to 2030, finding a significant global decline but a disproportionate burden in Africa.
articles.key_finding: Global pooled MDR-TB prevalence declined significantly from 14.4% (95% CI 9.0–19.8) in 2000–2009 to 2.6% (2.3–2.9) in 2020–2024.

articles.title: Epidemiology and Drug Resistance Patterns of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in High-Burden Area in Western Siberia, Russia.

Due to the longer duration of treatment and expensive second-line medicine, the economic burden of MDR-TB is assumed to be higher than drug-susceptible

response.global_summary:
The global age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) of tuberculosis (TB) significantly declined by **40.5%** from 1990 to 2021, decreasing from 173.0 to 103.0 per 100,000 population [4][5]. During the same period, the age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR) dropped from 40.0 to 14.0, and the age-standardized disability-adjusted life years (ASDR) decreased from 1,650.6 to 580.3 [4]. In 2023, approximately **10.6 million people** developed TB, leading to **1.6 million deaths** globally [7].

Despite the overall decline in TB incidence, multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) present a growing challenge [1]. The global ASIR of MDR-TB has not decreased since 2015 and has shown a slow upward trend in recent years [1]. Projections indicate that MDR-TB and XDR-TB are expected to see significant increases in both ASIR and ASMR from 2022 to 2035 [1]. A 30-year analysis of global trends also forecasts an uptick in MDR-TB incidence rates from 2020 to 2030 [0]. XDR-TB is emerging as the fastest-growing threat [3], with its ASIR exhibiting a significant increase over the past 30 years [1].

While the prevalence of MDR-TB among all TB patients globally showed a significant decline from **14.4%** in 2000–2009 to **2.6%** in 2020–2024 [2], the overall trends in MDR-TB have continued to accelerate, affecting more people [6]. The pooled odds of MDR-TB were **1.42 times higher** in HIV-positive patients compared to HIV-negative patients (OR=1.42, CI=1.17-1.71) [13]. In 2020, an estimated **500,000 new cases** of rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) occurred, but only **157,903 cases** were notified, indicating that only about a third of cases are detected and treated annually [10].

Drug-resistant TB, specifically multidrug-resistant TB excluding extensively drug-resistant TB, was among the top six pathogen-drug combinations causing **50,000-100,000 deaths** attributable to antimicrobial resistance (AMR) globally in 2019 [9]. New shorter, all-oral treatment regimens represent a breakthrough in TB management, but progress is threatened by rising resistance to bedaquiline [18].

Regionally, a cohort study in South Asia revealed significant declines in ASIR, age-standardized prevalence rate (ASPR), ASDR, and ASMR related to TB over the past three decades [17]. In contrast, a study in Western Siberia, Russia, observed a decrease in overall TB incidence from **93.9 to 48.1 per 100,000 population** between 2012 and 2021, but the primary MDR-TB rate *increased* from **19.2% to 26.4%** [11]. Urbanization scores in China were associated with a **1.1% reduction** in TB incidence per unit score [19].

key_findings.text: The global age-standardized incidence rate of tuberculosis (TB) decreased by 40.5% from 1990 to 2021, with corresponding declines in mortality and disability-adjusted life years.

The global age-standardized incidence rate of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) has not decreased since 2015 and shows a slow upward trend, with projections indicating significant increases in both incidence and mortality for MDR-TB and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) from 2022 to 2035.
Extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) is emerging as the fastest-growing threat, with its age-standardized incidence rate significantly increasing over the past 30 years.
The global pooled prevalence of MDR-TB among all TB patients declined significantly from 14.4% in 2000–2009 to 2.6% in 2020–2024.
HIV-positive patients have 1.42 times higher odds of developing MDR-TB compared to HIV-negative patients.
A significant portion of estimated new rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) cases are not detected and treated annually, with only about a third of cases notified in 2020.
Multidrug-resistant TB (excluding extensively drug-resistant TB) was among the leading causes of deaths attributable to bacterial antimicrobial resistance globally in 2019.
New shorter, all-oral treatment regimens for TB are a breakthrough, but their effectiveness is threatened by rising resistance to bedaquiline.
In Western Siberia, Russia, while overall TB incidence decreased, the primary MDR-TB rate increased from 19.2% to 26.4% between 2012 and 2021.

evidence_gaps: The sources do not provide a comprehensive global overview of the prevalence of pre-XDR-TB or XDR-TB among MDR-TB cases, only a pooled proportion from 22 countries [15].
The specific factors contributing to the projected increase in MDR-TB and XDR-TB incidence and mortality are not detailed in these sources.

The sources do not provide detailed information on the effectiveness or implementation challenges of new shorter, all-oral treatment regimens for TB, beyond noting the threat of bedaquiline resistance [18].

The sources do not consistently report the current global incidence rates for MDR-TB and XDR-TB, making it difficult to quantify the exact burden of these specific forms of drug-resistant TB in recent years.
The sources do not provide a detailed analysis of regional disparities in MDR-TB and XDR-TB trends beyond a few specific examples (e.g., Western Siberia [11], South Asia [17]).
